newsitem.title: FRANCE: CYCLING-FRAGILE ZUELLE SAYS HE IS NOT TIME TRIAL FAVOURITE.
newsitem.headline: CYCLING-FRAGILE ZUELLE SAYS HE IS NOT TIME TRIAL FAVOURITE.

text.p: World champion Alex Zuelle refuses to accept the label of favourite for the 7.3-km time trial that raises the curtain on the 84th Tour de France on Saturday.
The Swiss time trial specialist will start the 3,950-km Tour gingerly with 12 surgical pins holding together a collarbone that fractured in five places two weeks ago.
Before his crash in the Tour of Switzerland Zuelle was happy to be tipped to repeat last year's Tour success in the Dutch town of Hertogenbosch.
"Now there is no pressure on me," he said. "I intend to ride the first 10 days carefully. If everything is okay maybe I will have some energy for the mountains but if things are bad I may go home."
Last year he averaged 51.75 kph to beat Britain's Chris Boardman by two seconds on a rain-dampened day. Three months later he repeated the performance to win the world time trial title in Lugano.
Boardman is still trying to bury memories of the 1995 prologue time trial in Saint Brieuc. Then he crashed out, fracturing a wrist and ankle.
That wiped out dreams of another yellow-jersey triumph which his Tour debut brought three years ago.

"I am very happy with the circuit," Boardman said. "Even if it rains it will be okay because it is not technically difficult. It is as good as I could ask for. There is a hill but it is nothing much."
He has trained over the course which does not have too many corners to test the grip of tyres especially if the rain of past days continues.
The route takes the 198 riders over two bridges straddling the Seine and past the 12th century cathedral.
Switzerland have a knack of producing speed specialists such as Zuelle and former world hour record-breaker Tony Rominger.
Their latest find, Oscar Camenzind, is also coy about the prologue time trial.
"It's not my kind of circuit. I prefer plenty of corners," said the second-year professional who was robbed of winning last month's Tour of Switzerland because of a tactical error by his team.
Most of the major contenders include against-the-clock experts such as Spain's Abraham Olano, second in the world time trial two years ago.
They prefer however to conserve their strength for more important days ahead.
As the Tour this week remembers the 10th anniversary of the death of Jacques Anquetil, one of its greatest exponents and a time trial specialist, it also celebrates another significant date.
The prologue was invented by the Tour 30 years ago to give starting venues something extra for their investment.
However these short, sharp races against the clock came a year too late for the Rouen-born Anquetil.

Since 1967, when Spain's Jose Miguel Errandonea won the first one at Angers, the prologues have found a niche in Tour statistics even though they are regarded as a commercial gimmick by some die-hards.
